narrative:
The model estimated a 97% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt, so your law school application was denied. This is a probability-based screening decision, not a finding that you cannot succeed, but it means your profile was assessed as very high risk under the patterns the model learned.

The strongest factor was your third-year class-standing decile: you were in the lowest decile, while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile. That gap pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. Your LSAT score was the second most influential factor: at 23.5, it is well below the accepted-student average of about 37.2, and it also pushed toward failure. Third was your first-year class-standing decile: again at the lowest level versus an accepted average near the sixth decile, adding further risk. Together these academic indicators outweighed other information and drove the denial.

To move forward, focus on strengthening the areas most within your control: build a structured LSAT retake plan and seek academic advising or a preparation pathway that can demonstrate improved readiness. Ask whether the school offers human review or feedback, and consider reapplying after you have stronger test scores and evidence of academic improvement.
